title: The Tower with Three Windows: Heliopolis to the Fairy Tree
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Heliopolis: The Tower with Two Windows

stops.name: Baalbek, born among the temples of Baal-Hadad and Jupiter
stops.campa: Barbara is born into wealth in Phoenician Heliopolis, in the reign of Maximian, daughter of the high-ranking Roman official Dioscorus. The city holds the grandest architectures of the age: the vast podium of Jupiter Heliopolitanus rising over the old ground of Canaanite Baal-Hadad, courts of red granite columns hauled from Aswan, the Great Altar smoking with incense for a god who has worn three names (Baal, Zeus, Jupiter) and lost none of his thunder. The infant grows inside this weight of stone, a child of privilege in a city built to house a storm-god's residence on earth.
suggested_refs: The Temple of Jupiter Heliopolitanus, Baalbek, largest Roman temple podium in the ancient world

stops.name: Baalbek, the beauty that draws suitors
stops.campa: Barbara grows into a beauty spoken of beyond her father's house, and Dioscorus, proud and possessive, turns away one suitor after another, unwilling to see her married beneath her station or given to any man he has not chosen himself. Rome's Great Persecution gathers on the horizon of empire, edicts against the Christians nailed up in every provincial forum, and Heliopolis, city of Jupiter's grandest altar, is no safe air for the new faith. Dioscorus resolves on a stronger wall than refusal: a tower, to hold what is his until he alone decides its use.
suggested_refs: The Diocletianic Persecution edicts of 303 AD, the backdrop of Dioscorus's fear

stops.name: Baalbek, the tower with two windows
stops.campa: Dioscorus has a giant stone tower built to isolate his daughter from suitors and from the proselytizing Christians who have begun to trouble the province. He orders it built with two windows only, enough light for a life and no more, and sets Barbara within it as a jewel is set in a box. From its height she watches Heliopolis go about its pagan business: the sacrifices, the fairs, the ordinary unremarkable idolatry of a whole city, and begins, in the narrowness of her captivity, to want more light than two windows give.
suggested_refs: Barbara's tower with three windows, the central image of her iconography

stops.name: Baalbek, the priest disguised as a physician
stops.campa: Word of a walled-up heiress reaches the clandestine Christians of the province, and a priest comes to Heliopolis got up as a travelling physician, admitted to the tower on the pretext of tending the lady's health. Behind the excuse of medicine he opens to her the mysteries of the faith: the Trinity, the Incarnation, the water that washes what no physician can touch, and she is catechized in secret, session by session, and baptized within her father's own walls before the disguised priest returns to his country and vanishes from the record.
suggested_refs: The Golden Legend's account of the priest sent in the guise of a physician

segments.name: The Voyage and the Third Window

stops.name: Baalbek, Dioscorus departs, and the third window is coerced
stops.campa: Dioscorus leaves on a long voyage, entrusting the finishing of a private bath-house near the tower to his workmen, with instructions for two windows as before. While he is away Barbara goes to the masons and, over their hesitation, persuades and then commands them: make me here another window. They cut the third opening into the stone. It is a small act of will inside a father's absence, and it is the whole of the rebellion: three lights admitted into a house built for two, and nothing yet said aloud about why.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara
suggested_refs: The three-windowed tower, the fixed attribute of Barbara in Christian art from the 14th century onward

stops.name: Baalbek, the Holy Spirit through the third window, the idols broken
stops.campa: Through the new-cut third window the Holy Spirit descends on Barbara as light descends, filling the bath-house and the tower above it with a presence her father's architecture was never built to hold. In that filling she rises and goes through the rooms overturning what her father worships: the household idols of Baal-Hadad and Jupiter that furnish every Heliopolitan house of standing are broken, thrown down, unmade, one after another, until the tower that was raised to keep the Trinity out has become the first temple in the city built, unknowingly, in its honor.
suggested_refs: The descent of the Spirit through the third window, depicted beside the broken idols in later Passio manuscripts

stops.name: Baalbek, Dioscorus returns and questions the altered tower
stops.campa: Dioscorus comes home from his voyage and sees at once what has been done to his building: three windows where he left two, the household gods lying broken on the floor. He goes down with his daughter into the bath-house and demands of her how three windows can give more light than two, sensing already, before she answers, that the question is not really about light. Barbara stands before her father in the room he built to contain her and does not retreat from what she has made.
stops.quote: I have done them to be made because three windows lighten all the world and all creatures, but two make darkness.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara
suggested_refs: Piscine/bath-house scenes of the confrontation, a recurring panel in Barbara altarpieces

stops.name: Baalbek, she declares the Trinity, and his fury
stops.campa: Barbara answers her father plainly: the three windows betoken the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, three persons and one very true God, on whom we ought to believe and worship, and that her betrothed is the crucified Messiah, that the three lights shed light on the whole world through the power of the Trinity. Dioscorus, hearing his daughter name the executed god of a persecuted sect as her husband, draws his sword in the same breath. She does not recant. She turns and runs, and he comes after her with the blade still bare.
stops.quote: These three windows betoken clearly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, the which be three persons and one very true God, on whom we ought to believe and worship.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara
suggested_refs: Iconography of Barbara with chalice, host, and the tower of three windows together, the Trinity made visible

stops.name: The mountain above Heliopolis, the pursuit
stops.campa: Barbara flees the tower and the city, out past the last temple courts and into the foothills where the Anti-Lebanon rises toward the snow, her father coming behind her with the sword he drew in the bath-house. She runs as a woman runs who has just told the truth for the first time in her life and finds it has cost her everything at once: father, house, safety, and gained her nothing yet but the running itself. The mountain closes around her like a held breath, and ahead of her the rock face shows no door.
suggested_refs: The wilderness flight, a fixed episode of the Passio between the Trinity confession and the capture

stops.name: The mountain cleft, the rock opens and closes around her
stops.campa: At the blank face of the cliff Barbara's road runs out, and the Lord commands the rock to part for her. The stone opens along a seam that was not there a moment before, and she enters the cleft of the mountain, tunneling up into the living rock itself; the cliff closes behind her and carries her, hidden inside the mountain's own body, to a hollow near its crown, from which she can look down, unseen, on the city that made her and the father who is hunting her through it.
suggested_refs: The parted rock of the mountain, patroness Barbara's tie to subterranean work and mining

stops.name: The mountain pasture, the shepherd's betrayal
stops.campa: Two shepherds have watched the whole of it from their flocks on the slope: the sword, the running girl, the rock parting and shutting like a door with no hinge. Dioscorus finds them and asks after his daughter. The first will not say. The second, for the promise of a reward, points out the way she went and is paid for it at once: his flock of sheep is turned to a plague of locusts before his eyes, and the shepherd himself is turned to stone on the hillside where he stood to sell her.
suggested_refs: The petrified shepherd and the locust-flock, a folk-punishment episode attached to the flight

stops.name: Baalbek, dragged home by the hair
stops.campa: With the betrayed path before him, Dioscorus climbs to the hollow in the rock and seizes his daughter by the hair. He drags her down the mountain and back through the streets of Heliopolis she once watched only from a window, past the temples she helped to empty, and returns her to the tower he built for her safety and now uses as her prison. He locks the door on the room with three windows in it, and the same light that once carried the Spirit into the house now only shows her the walls.
suggested_refs: The tower-prison, reused now as punishment rather than seclusion

stops.name: Baalbek tower, disrobed and beaten bloody
stops.campa: Locked within the tower, Barbara is stripped and beaten by her father's hand until she lies in her own blood on the floor she once filled with broken idols. Dioscorus punishes the body of the daughter he cannot argue out of her God, striking her the way a man strikes a wall that will not fall, wound after wound, until he leaves her for dead or near it on the stone. Nothing in the room answers him: not the three windows, not the light through them, only his daughter's silence under the blows and her refusal, even bleeding, to unsay what she said.
suggested_refs: The scourging of Barbara within the tower, one of the standard scenes of her martyrdom cycle

stops.name: Baalbek tower, the wounds healed by morning
stops.campa: Barbara wakes in the locked room to find the wounds of the night before closed and whole, her skin unmarked where her father's blows opened it, as if the beating had been erased along with the night. It is the first of the healings that will punctuate every torture still to come: her faith answered each morning with a body restored, so that no single day's cruelty can be made to stand as the last word on her. Dioscorus, informed of it, does not relent; he escalates, and delivers her at last to the machinery of the state.
suggested_refs: The nightly-healed wounds, the recurring miracle of the Passio's torture sequence

stops.name: Baalbek, delivered to the prefect Marcianus; torches and iron claws
stops.campa: After a grievous imprisonment Dioscorus hands his daughter over to Marcianus, the provincial prefect, to be broken by the machinery of Roman law where a father's fists have failed. She is stripped again, struck with whips and clubs until she stands in a pool of her own blood, her sides raked with claws of iron, and torches held to her flesh to burn away her faith along with her skin. The torches go out of themselves as they near her; her wounds, examined the next morning, are healed entire, and the soldiers who rub vinegar into her cuts cannot find where the cuts were.
suggested_refs: The torches that extinguish themselves near the martyr, and the iron claws of the standard iconography

stops.name: Baalbek, Juliana converted, tortured beside her
stops.campa: A young woman named Juliana, imprisoned already for her own confession of Christ, watches Barbara's wounds close overnight and is so struck by the sight that she declares herself ready to suffer whatever comes, come what may, for the same God who heals what the prefect's men break. Marcianus, seeing a second convert made out of his own torture chamber, orders Juliana bound and beaten alongside Barbara, and the two women go into the remaining torments together: one strengthened by the other's testimony, both refusing, under the same iron and the same fire, to unsay their faith.
suggested_refs: Saint Juliana of Heliopolis, martyred beside Barbara and commemorated with her on the same feast

stops.name: Baalbek, mutilation, burning, dragged through the streets
stops.campa: Marcianus orders what remains of mercy stripped away: Barbara is mutilated, her breasts cut off, her body burned with fire, and then dragged naked through the public streets of Heliopolis as a spectacle and a warning to any citizen who might follow her God. She is carried past the temple courts of her own childhood, past the tower with three windows still standing on its hill, and through it all her faith holds unwavering; each new cruelty leaves her recovered rather than broken, and the city that watches begins to understand that this prefect cannot win by inflicting pain.
suggested_refs: The severed-breast motif, shared across the legends of several virgin martyrs of this era

segments.name: The Judge and the Execution by Her Father's Hand

stops.name: Baalbek, condemned to death by the sword
stops.campa: Marcianus, unable to break Barbara by torture and unwilling to be shamed further by her endurance, brings her before the judge's seat a final time and pronounces the sentence Roman law reserves for the unrepentant: death by the sword, beheading, outside the city walls. Dioscorus, present at the sentencing, hears the verdict pass on his own daughter and does not ask for clemency; he asks instead for the office of executioner, offering to do with his own hand what the state has ordered done, so that the last authority over her body remains, as it began, his.
suggested_refs: The sentencing before Marcianus, prefect of Heliopolis, the last civil act of the Passio

stops.name: The mountain above Heliopolis, led out to the place of execution
stops.campa: Barbara and Juliana are led out of the city together to the mountainside, the same slope, tradition holds, where the rock once opened for her flight, to be beheaded outside the walls as the law requires. On the climb Barbara prays her last prayer aloud: that the Lord who formed heaven and earth hear all who keep memory of His name and of her passion, and not remember their sins, for He knows our fragility. It is the prayer that will make her, for a thousand years after, the saint invoked against a death that comes too suddenly for confession.
stops.quote: Lord Jesu Christ, which hast formed heaven and earth, I beseech thee to grant me thy grace and hear my prayer, that all they that have memory of thy name and my passion, I pray thee that thou wilt not remember their sins, for thou knowest our fragility.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara
suggested_refs: Barbara's dying prayer, the theological root of her patronage against sudden and unconfessed death

stops.name: The mountainside, Dioscorus claims the sword
stops.campa: On the mountain Dioscorus takes up the sword himself rather than let a stranger's hand finish what his own hand began in the bath-house. He beheads his daughter on the fourth of December, the day the Church will keep as her feast for as long as it keeps feasts, while beside them the appointed executioner beheads Juliana. Barbara dies by the hand that built her tower, gave her two windows, and could not forgive her the third: the whole architecture of the father's love turned, at the very end, into the instrument of her death.
suggested_refs: 4 December, the feast of Saint Barbara, fixed on the day of her death by tradition

stops.name: The mountainside, the lightning, and Dioscorus burned to ash
stops.campa: As Dioscorus and Juliana's executioner come down from the mountain, the heavens open without warning and a fire falls from the sky: a bolt of lightning strikes Dioscorus where he walks and consumes him to ashes on the path, and a second bolt takes the man who beheaded Juliana. Marcianus, hearing how the two executioners died within the hour of the executions, is seized with such terror that he too dies of the fright. The court that condemned her does not survive the day of her death; the sky itself closes the account the law left open.
suggested_refs: The lightning bolt consuming Dioscorus, the root of Barbara's patronage over storms, artillery, and sudden fire from heaven

segments.name: The Cult Across a Thousand Years

stops.name: Constantinople, the relics translated from Heliopolis
stops.campa: In the sixth century, as the empire that once tried her rebuilds itself as Christian Byzantium, the relics of the Great Martyr Barbara are translated from Heliopolis to Constantinople, carried out of the province where she was born and beheaded into the capital of the faith her father tried to wall out of his house. The tower with three windows has by now become an image known across the Greek-speaking world; the girl once dragged by the hair through Heliopolis's streets is received into the City of Constantine under incense and imperial ceremony, a martyr promoted at last to the center of the world that killed her.
suggested_refs: The Translation of the Relics of Saint Barbara, kept as its own feast in the Orthodox calendar

stops.name: Kyiv, the relics at Saint Michael's Golden-Domed Monastery
stops.campa: Tradition brings the relics further still: a Byzantine princess named Barbara, said to be daughter of the Emperor Alexios Komnenos, marries a prince of Rus and carries the martyr's bones north with her into Kyiv, where they are enshrined at the Golden-Domed Monastery of Saint Michael. There they remain through the centuries of the Rus church, an Akathist sung before them every week, the hand of the saint kept in its own reliquary at the monastery's left side: the third sister of the essay's triad now resident in a city her own hagiography never imagined, still working the healing she worked in her father's tower.
suggested_refs: The relics of Saint Barbara, later moved to St. Vladimir's Cathedral, Kyiv, where an Akathist is sung every Tuesday

stops.name: Regensburg, the Fourteen Holy Helpers gathered against the plague
stops.campa: In the dioceses of Regensburg, Bamberg, and Würzburg, amid the Black Death and the famine that rides beside it, the faithful begin to invoke a fixed company of fourteen saints together as a single wall against plague, sudden death, and the collapse of the ordinary protections of life. Barbara stands at the core of the group with Margaret and Catherine, the three virgin martyrs of the Levant, contemporaries born two hundred kilometers from one another, now recruited as captains in a company of celestial specialists, each with a proprietary power, invoked as a body against a century that has run out of other defenses.
suggested_refs: The earliest Regensburg-area prayers and monastery images of the Fourteen Holy Helpers as a fixed group

stops.name: Kutná Hora, the miners raise the Church of Saint Barbara
stops.campa: In the Bohemian silver town of Kutná Hora, whose entire wealth rises out of the veins its miners open in the rock, the miners' guild lays the first stones of a church to Barbara, patroness of subterranean work since the mountain once opened and closed around her, raising over decades a Gothic hall so vast and so ambitious it will not be finished for over five centuries. Frescoes inside will one day show the miners themselves at their work, offering their labor upward to the saint who tunneled into living stone and came out unharmed on the other side.
suggested_refs: St. Barbara's Church, Kutná Hora, UNESCO World Heritage Site, built by the town's silver-mining guild

stops.name: Antwerp, Jan van Eyck draws Barbara before her unfinished tower
stops.campa: In the Low Countries the painter Jan van Eyck signs and dates a small panel of Saint Barbara seated in the foreground, reading, while behind her rises a tower still under construction, scaffolding and half-cut stone visible against the sky: the tower with three windows caught, uniquely in her whole iconographic tradition, in the act of being built rather than finished. The panel is left as a drawing under a thin grisaille wash, whether by design or interruption no one now can say, an unfinished image of an unfinished tower for a saint whose story is itself about a room completed against instruction.
suggested_refs: Jan van Eyck, Saint Barbara, 1437, Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (KMSKA)

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the shepherd's vision, the fourteen children
stops.campa: Above the Cistercian abbey of Langheim in Franconia, the shepherd Hermann Leicht sees a crying child in the field and, stooping to lift it, watches it vanish; the vision returns weeks later with two burning candles beside it, and then, in June, a third time, bearing a red cross on its breast and surrounded by thirteen other children. We are the fourteen helpers, the child declares, and wish to erect a chapel here, where we can rest. Barbara stands among them as she has stood in Regensburg's prayers for a century, and the basilica that will one day rise on this field is named, simply, for the Fourteen.
stops.quote: We are the fourteen helpers, and wish to erect a chapel here, where we can rest. If you will be our servant, we will be yours.
stops.quote_source: The apparition to Hermann Leicht, June 1446, as preserved in the Langheim abbey tradition
suggested_refs: The Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers (Vierzehnheiligen), built 1743-1772 on the site of the apparition

stops.name: Segovia, the Real Colegio de Artillería names her patroness
stops.campa: In the Alcázar of Segovia, on the sixteenth of May, Lieutenant General Félix Gazola founds the Real Colegio de Artillería under Charles III, and the corps takes as its patroness the saint whose father was struck down by fire from the open sky: Barbara, invoked against the same thunder her tower's third window let in, now invoked for the controlled thunder of the gun. Every fourth of December the Academy keeps her feast as its own: cannon that answer to a name first spoken over a girl who converted her father's household gods into rubble before he ever raised a sword against her.
suggested_refs: Santa Bárbara, patrona del Arma de Artillería, 4 December, Real Colegio de Artillería de Segovia

stops.name: Obernburg am Main, the Annakapelle and the verse of the three holy maids
stops.campa: Fifty kilometers up the Main from Frankfurt, in the little chapel of Saint Anne at Obernburg, a Nothelferaltar carved by Peter Vambach of Erlenbach sets Christ at the center of the Fourteen Helpers in four ranked rows, and beside it a plaque still carries the old rhyme of the three virgin sisters: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl: those are the three holy maids. It is the same verse the essay's own accounting begins from, the mnemonic that keeps the tower-bearer bound in memory to the dragon-slayer and the wheel-breaker, three names that will not come apart.
stops.quote: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl, das sind die drei heiligen Madl.
stops.quote_source: Plaque verse, Annakapelle, Obernburg am Main
suggested_refs: The Nothelferaltar of the Annakapelle, Obernburg am Main, and its verse of the three holy maids

stops.name: Madrid, the Museo Naval and the santabárbara of every Spanish ship
stops.campa: The Museo Naval opens in Madrid, gathering the models and relics of a navy whose every ship still calls its magazine of powder and shell by her name: the santabárbara, the compartment where the explosive heart of a warship is kept, named for the saint invoked against lightning and sudden detonation since her father was burned to ash on the mountain outside Heliopolis. In the museum's halls the models of the Santa Ana and the Santísima Trinidad carry, unmarked but understood by every sailor who served aboard them, a small stone room bearing a name that began as a tower with three windows.
suggested_refs: The santabárbara, the powder magazine of the Spanish and Hispanic naval tradition, Museo Naval de Madrid

stops.name: Weimar, the fourteen angels of the evening prayer
stops.campa: At the Deutsches Nationaltheater in Weimar, Richard Strauss conducts the premiere of Engelbert Humperdinck's Hänsel und Gretel, and the children of the opera sing their evening prayer into the lost forest: fourteen angels stand about me while I sleep. The line descends from the same Franconian devotion born at Langheim and carried down every German nursery since: Barbara's own company, numbered exactly, now watching over two children who, like her, are alone in a wood ruled by a hostile power. In this city of Goethe's own house the fourteen helpers step, briefly, out of chapel and into song.
suggested_refs: Engelbert Humperdinck, Hänsel und Gretel (1893), the Abendsegen and its fourteen guardian angels

segments.name: The Interpolation: Barbara Restored to the Fairy Tree

stops.name: Domrémy, the Ladies' Tree, the third sister among the garlands
stops.campa: Under the great beech the country calls the Ladies' Tree, near the well Joffrey de Bourlémont built two hundred years before, the child Jehanne sings and dances with the other children of Domrémy and Greux, weaving garlands of flower and leaf for Our Lady and for whatever else still listens in that field. The trial record will keep only two of the three virgin martyrs at her side, Catherine and Margaret; but Katrin Vates's embroidery of this same hillside restores what the parchment dropped: Barbara, tower-bearer, third sister of the Heliopolitan triad, present at the tree with her sisters from the very beginning, the interpolation that fills a lacuna in a poem that rhymes.
suggested_refs: Katrin Vates (Ekaterina Sinchinova), 'Domrémy' embroidery, January 2023, the tree, the well, and the tower
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json, the Tree of Bourlemont stop (same pin)

stops.name: Domrémy, the tower over the field, the black window
stops.campa: On her own feast day, the fourth of December, the maiden of the tower keeps her appointment at the stone tower Joffrey de Bourlémont raised a lifetime before as a seat of grief and now finds turned to a house of annunciation. Joan climbs to it by night and communes there with Barbara, who teaches her the science of artillery and the opening of portals: the same rock-parting power that once carried a fleeing girl into a mountain in Heliopolis, now teaching a French girl how a black window opens in a wall, framed by lightning, and what it means to be one and the same with every maiden ever shut in a tower.
suggested_refs: Saint Barbara with her tower, patroness of artillery, the maiden of the black window, Lois de Conte's account
sources: joffrey_bourlemont.journey.json, 'The tower, Saint Barbara and the black window' (same pin, same date)

stops.name: Orléans, Les Tourelles, standing behind the Maid's cannon
stops.campa: Before the bridge-fort of the Tourelles, where the guns of the deliverance of Orléans speak all day into the English works and an arrow finds Jehanne above the breast exactly as she foretold it would, the gunners' saint stands unseen behind the Maid's own artillery, the tower-bearer who taught her the science of the cannon now present at the discharge of it, patroness of the thing she once suffered under a different name: fire that falls without warning and changes everything it touches. When the standard's tail brushes the wall and the fort falls in a rush, it is Barbara's ordnance as much as France's that has spoken.
suggested_refs: Santa Bárbara, patroness of artillery, standing invisibly beside the Maid's guns at the Tourelles
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json, 'Les Tourelles, the wound and the fall of the bridge-fort' (same pin, same date)
